props.title: Diamonds

sections.content: Diamonds represents an interesting late-career turn for Kirk Douglas, tackling the role of a former boxing champion recovering from a stroke - a particularly poignant performance given Douglas's real-life stroke in 1996. The film pairs him with Dan Aykroyd in a heist-meets-redemption story that echoes earlier boxing classics like The Set-Up (1949) and Champion (1949), while incorporating elements of crime capers like Ocean's 11 (1960). Though not as celebrated as Douglas's iconic roles in Spartacus (1960) or Paths of Glory (1957), it showcases his remarkable resilience and determination to continue acting despite physical challenges.

sections.content: The diamond heist element of the film connects it to a rich tradition of jewel theft movies, from the sophisticated To Catch a Thief (1955) to the grittier Thief (1981). The father-son dynamic between Douglas and Aykroyd taps into similar territory as Color of Money (1986), where an aging expert teams up with a younger partner for one last score. The Canadian setting and involvement of organized crime also brings to mind elements of Force of Evil (1948) and The Silent Partner (1978). SUBHEAD: Late Career Performances and Physical Challenges

Douglas's performance in Diamonds joins other notable late-career roles by Hollywood legends who continued working despite health challenges, like John Wayne in The Shootist (1976) and Henry Fonda in On Golden Pond (1981). The film's treatment of aging and physical recovery parallels themes explored in Rocky Balboa (2006) and The Wrestler (2008), where former athletes confront their limitations while maintaining their dignity.
